To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
reading factual texts activates the brain regions involved in the reconstruction of events, while reading fiction activates the regions involved in imagining possible events.
reading fiction and reading fact are associated with different neural activation patterns and behavioral effects.
the brain regions involved in action simulation and imagination are engaged in the reading of both factual and fictional stories, respectively.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how we read and understand stories and how we differentiate between factual and fictional contents.
the neural and cognitive mechanisms underlying the reading of fiction and nonfiction.
the question whether the reading of factual or fictional stories engages different neurocognitive processes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
reading fiction is a constructive process that is not only based on a reconstruction of what has been read, but also includes a prediction of what might have been.

the reading of fiction engages the reader in a constructive simulation of the depicted events and that reading factual stories engages the reader in an action-oriented reconstruction of the events described.

reading in a factual mode is associated with the activation of the default mode network and the reading of fiction is associated with the simulation of possible events, which is supported by the activation of the mentalizing network.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

reading factual stories is a process in which we try to reconstruct the events that actually took place, whereas reading fictional stories is a process where we simulate the events that might have happened.

we can distinguish between two modes of reading: one is based on the past-oriented reconstruction of real-life events (factual), the other is based on the construction of what might have been (fictional).
reading fiction engages the reader in a constructive process, whereas reading facts engages the reader in an action-based reconstruction process.
The main takeaway from our work is that
reading a story in a factual mode is not just a matter of reading a text, but rather of reconstructing an event in the past, whereas the reading of fiction seems to be more a process of imagination.
reading fiction is not a simple passive reception of information but rather an active construction process.
the brain processes factual and fictional information differently, even if they are presented in a comparable way.
